# Onu 0.1.0: full documentation

---

## Rules

### Before writing code

- Look up a component's page before using it: `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/docs/<group>/<name>.md`, `onu_get_doc` in the MCP server, or the site's `llms.txt`. Each page has a **Props** table and an **Accessibility** section. Use only the props listed there.
- Prefer an Onu component over writing your own or using a shadcn/ui primitive directly. `llms.txt` lists every component with one line on what it is for. Only reach for `@javaabu/onu/primitives` (the shadcn/ui parts Onu is built on) to compose something Onu doesn't have.
- Don't add other UI kits (MUI, Chakra, Ant Design, Headless UI, a separate shadcn/ui copy) next to Onu.

### Setup

- One CSS entry: `@import "tailwindcss"; @import "@javaabu/onu/tailwind.css";` and, for the font pack, `@import "@javaabu/onu/fonts.css";`, which needs `npm install @fontsource-variable/inter @fontsource-variable/jetbrains-mono @fontsource-variable/noto-sans-thaana` first.
- Wrap the app once in `<ThemeProvider><OnuProvider>…</OnuProvider></ThemeProvider>`. `OnuProvider` sets `lang`, `dir` and density on `<html>`, so portals follow.
- Dhivehi: `locale={dv}` with `import { dv } from "@javaabu/onu/locales/dv"`, or `locale="dv"` to load it on demand. English needs no `locale`.
- Inertia or Next.js: pass the router's `Link` as `linkComponent` on `OnuProvider`; Onu's links and `href` props then use it.

### Imports

- Components, hooks and helpers come from `@javaabu/onu`. Heavy features have their own entry: `@javaabu/onu/charts`, `/maps`, `/editor`, `/calendar`, `/media`, `/query-builder`, `/export`, `/thaana`, `/icons/iconify`, `/icons/fontawesome`. The docs page's first code block shows the import.
- Never import from `@javaabu/onu/dist/...` or `@javaabu/onu/src/...`.

### Forms (Laravel)

- Put every control inside `FormField` with the field's `name` (bracket notation is fine, `items[0][name]`). `FormField` wires the label, help, errors and ARIA. Don't hand-write `<label>`, error text or `aria-describedby`.
- Use `Form` with an `onSubmit` that returns the request promise (axios, fetch or Inertia). It shows Laravel 422 errors under the fields, focuses the first one and shows the error summary. With Inertia, pass `errors={form.errors}` and `processing={form.processing}`.
- Submit with `SubmitButton` (spinner, no double submit), not a plain `Button type="submit"`.
- Pick the specific input: `EmailInput`, `PasswordInput`, `PhoneInput`, `NumberInput`, `DatePicker`, `ApiSelect` (Laravel paginated API), `InstantFileUpload`, and so on, rather than `TextInput type="…"`.
- Edit pages get `SaveBar`; index pages get `ListingPage` (or `DataTable` with `useListingState`).

### Dhivehi, Thaana and RTL

- Free-text fields that may hold Dhivehi take `thaana` (`<TextInput thaana />`, `<Textarea thaana />`), or use `ThaanaInput`. Never add `thaana` to email, password, URL, number, phone, OTP or code inputs; they stay LTR by design.
- Use logical Tailwind utilities only: `ms-*`/`me-*`, `ps-*`/`pe-*`, `start-*`/`end-*`, `text-start`/`text-end`, `border-s`/`border-e`, `rounded-s-*`/`rounded-e-*`. Never `ml-*`, `mr-*`, `pl-*`, `pr-*`, `left-*`, `right-*`, `text-left` or `text-right`. Flip transforms with `rtl:`.
- Sides are `side="start" | "end"`, not left/right.
- Format dates, numbers and money with `useFormatDate`, `useFormatNumber` and `useFormatCurrency` (MVR), not `toLocaleString` or hand-built strings. Numbers use Western digits in Dhivehi too.
- Built-in strings come from the locale. For your own strings use `useTranslation()` or your app's i18n, and override Onu's strings with `OnuProvider messages`.

### Styling and theming

- Brand colour: set `--onu-primary` (one variable re-themes everything). Use the theme tokens (`bg-background`, `text-foreground`, `bg-primary`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border`, `bg-card`, …), never fixed colours like `bg-blue-600` or hex values, so dark mode and themes keep working.
- Restyle with `className` (merged with tailwind-merge, yours wins) and `classNames={{ part: "…" }}` for parts. Reuse exported variants such as `buttonVariants`. Use `asChild` to render your own element. No `!important`, no inline styles for static values.
- Density (`compact` to `touch`) and dark mode come from the providers; don't hard-code heights or `dark:` colours on Onu components.

### Icons

- Use `<Icon name="search" />` and `startIcon="add"` / `endIcon="…"` props with semantic names, not imports from `lucide-react`. Give icons that carry meaning a `label`; icon-only buttons need an accessible name (`aria-label` or the component's `label` prop).
- Directional icons mirror in RTL on their own; don't flip them yourself.

### Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA)

- Onu components already handle roles, focus and keyboard. Don't remove focus rings, add `tabIndex` to non-interactive elements, or replace buttons with clickable `div`s.
- Announce async results with `toast()`, `announce()` or `LiveRegion`; hide text visually with `VisuallyHidden`, not `display: none`.
- Confirm destructive actions with `confirm()` / `useConfirm()` or the item's `confirm` option, not `window.confirm`.

### Bundle size

- Import only what you use; every entry is tree-shaken. Keep charts, maps, the editor, the calendar and media in their own entries (and lazy routes when they are big).

---

<!-- docs/intro.md -->

# Onu

[Onu](https://github.com/Javaabu/onu) is Javaabu's React UI component library. Onu (އޮނު) means _bamboo_ in Dhivehi.

It is built on [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com) and [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com), and adds what Javaabu projects need out of the box:

- every component works right-to-left, with Dhivehi strings, dates and fonts built in;
- every free-text field can type Thaana from a Latin keyboard;
- one CSS variable, `--onu-primary`, re-themes the whole library;
- dark mode, density modes (compact to touch) and responsive, touch-friendly components;
- WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility;
- Lucide icons by default, with FontAwesome Pro and Iconify adapters.

```tsx
import { FormField, OnuProvider, TextInput } from "@javaabu/onu"
import { dv } from "@javaabu/onu/locales/dv"

export function NameField() {
  return (
    <OnuProvider locale={dv}>
      <FormField label="ނަން" required>
        <TextInput thaana />
      </FormField>
    </OnuProvider>
  )
}
```

Browse every component and the sample pages in the [web app](https://onu.on-forge.com/).

---

<!-- docs/installation-and-setup.md -->

# Installation

First install the NPM package

```bash
npm install @javaabu/onu --save
```

# Styles

Import Tailwind and Onu's stylesheet in your main CSS file. The font pack is optional; to use it, first install the fonts it loads:

```bash
npm install @fontsource-variable/inter @fontsource-variable/jetbrains-mono @fontsource-variable/noto-sans-thaana
```

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@javaabu/onu/tailwind.css";
@import "@javaabu/onu/fonts.css"; /* optional: needs the font packages above */
```

Without the font pack, leave out the last line. Faruma and MV Faseyha (Thaana) are inside `@javaabu/onu`; see [Fonts](./guides/fonts.md).

`tailwind.css` adds Onu's design tokens, the dark mode variant, and tells Tailwind to scan Onu's components for classes.

# Providers

Wrap your app in `ThemeProvider` (light, dark and system themes) and `OnuProvider` (locale, direction, density, icons and links).

```tsx
import { OnuProvider, ThemeProvider } from "@javaabu/onu"
import { dv } from "@javaabu/onu/locales/dv"

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(
  <ThemeProvider>
    <OnuProvider locale={dv}>
      <App />
    </OnuProvider>
  </ThemeProvider>,
)
```

`OnuProvider` sets `lang`, `dir` and `data-density` on `<html>`, so dialogs and menus rendered in portals follow the same direction. Pass `syncDocument={false}` if Onu only controls part of a page.

English-only apps leave out `locale` and import nothing else: each component brings its own English text, so neither the Dhivehi strings nor the full English set end up in the bundle. `locale="dv"` also works and loads the Dhivehi text on demand (see [Dhivehi & locales](./guides/dhivehi-and-locales.md#loading-dhivehi)).

| Prop            | Default     | Description                                                        |
| --------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `locale`        | `"en"`      | A locale object (`dv` from `@javaabu/onu/locales/dv`), `"en"` or `"dv"` |
| `dir`           | from locale | Override the direction                                             |
| `messages`      |             | Override individual strings, e.g. `{ common: { save: "Submit" } }` |
| `density`       | `"default"` | `"compact"`, `"default"`, `"comfortable"` or `"touch"`             |
| `labelLayout`   | `"stacked"` | Default label layout for form fields: `"stacked"` or `"inline"`    |
| `linkComponent` | `"a"`       | Component used for links, e.g. Inertia's or Next's `Link`          |
| `icons`         | Lucide      | Map semantic icon names to another set, e.g. FontAwesome Pro (the default Lucide set loads on demand) |
| `iconSources`   |             | Icon sources for `DynamicIcon` and the icon picker                 |
| `maps`          |             | `{ googleMapsApiKey, mapId, darkMapId }`                           |

# Laravel + Inertia

```tsx
import { Link } from "@inertiajs/react"

;<OnuProvider linkComponent={Link}>…</OnuProvider>
```

Pass Inertia's `errors` to forms with `FormErrorsProvider` so every field shows its validation errors. See [Forms & Laravel validation](./guides/forms-and-laravel.md).

# Avoiding a theme flash (SSR)

Add `themeScript()` to `<head>` so the stored theme applies before the first paint:

```tsx
import { themeScript } from "@javaabu/onu"

;<script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: themeScript() }} />
```

---

<!-- docs/guides/design-and-density.md -->

# Design & density

Onu's default look pairs a Proton Mail-style app shell with Ant Design 5 content elements: 14px text, 32px controls, 6px control corners and 8px cards, hairline borders, plain greys, and colour used for emphasis. Only popups cast a (subtle) shadow. See [Theming](./theming.md#the-default-look) for the tokens behind it. The same components work for admin panels, public portals, learning platforms and kiosks; density modes adapt them.

# Density modes

| Mode | Use for | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `compact` | Data-heavy tables and grids | Tighter spacing (about 10% smaller) |
| `default` | Admin forms and pages | Ant Design's default size: 32px controls, 12px 16px table cells |
| `comfortable` | Public and citizen portals, LMS | More generous spacing |
| `touch` | Kiosks | Large targets (buttons ≥ 44px) and larger text |

Set it for the whole app or for part of a page:

```tsx
<OnuProvider density="comfortable">…</OnuProvider>

<Density value="compact">
    <DataTable … />
</Density>
```

Density scales Tailwind's spacing unit, so every size in a subtree follows: paddings, gaps, heights and icon sizes.

# Responsive

Every component works from 320px phones to large screens. Many adapt to the space they are in (container queries) rather than the screen size, so a form in a narrow sidebar stacks even on a wide monitor. Built-in patterns include tables that become labelled cards on phones, filter panels that become bottom sheets, sidebars that become drawers, and save bars that become bottom bars.

# Fluid type

App screens use Tailwind's fixed type scale. Portal and marketing pages (heroes, landing pages, feature sections) can use the fluid scale instead (R3.4): each step grows smoothly from a 320px to a 1280px wide viewport with `clamp()`. The sizes are mostly `rem`, so they still follow browser zoom.

| Utility           | 320px    | 1280px   | Line height | Use for                       |
| ----------------- | -------- | -------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| `text-fluid-sm`   | 0.875rem | 1rem     | normal      | Small print                   |
| `text-fluid-base` | 1rem     | 1.125rem | normal      | Body text on portal pages     |
| `text-fluid-lg`   | 1.125rem | 1.375rem | normal      | Lead paragraphs               |
| `text-fluid-xl`   | 1.25rem  | 1.75rem  | snug        | Card and sub-section headings |
| `text-fluid-2xl`  | 1.5rem   | 2.25rem  | snug        | Section headings              |
| `text-fluid-3xl`  | 1.875rem | 3rem     | tight       | Page headings                 |
| `text-fluid-4xl`  | 2.25rem  | 3.75rem  | tight       | Hero headings                 |
| `text-fluid-5xl`  | 2.5rem   | 4.5rem   | tight       | Large hero headings           |

```tsx
<h2 className="text-fluid-2xl font-semibold">Popular services</h2>
<p className="text-fluid-lg text-muted-foreground">Apply, pay and track requests online.</p>
```

Each utility sets a matching line height. Under `lang="dv"` the line heights are taller (tight 1.5, snug 1.6, normal 1.8) so Thaana fili are never clipped. The utilities merge with `cn()` as font sizes, so `cn("text-sm", "text-fluid-xl")` keeps only the fluid size.

The values are CSS variables, so a project can retune any step without Tailwind config:

```css
:root {
  --onu-text-fluid-5xl: clamp(3rem, 2rem + 4vw, 6rem);
}
```

Without Tailwind (`@javaabu/onu/styles.css`), use the variables directly: `font-size: var(--fluid-text-3xl); line-height: var(--fluid-leading-tight)`. [Hero](../layout-and-navigation/hero.md) uses this scale.

# Touch

On touch screens (`pointer: coarse`) buttons, inputs and menu items are at least 44px tall whatever the density. Nothing relies on hover alone, gestures (swipe, drag to dismiss, pinch) always have a button alternative, and fixed bars respect the notch and home indicator (safe-area insets).

Use the `touch:` variant for your own touch-specific styles: `touch:min-h-11`.

---

<!-- docs/guides/theming.md -->

# The default look

Onu's default theme pairs a Proton Mail-style app shell with Ant Design 5 content elements:

- **Brand**: Proton purple `#6d4aff` (`oklch(0.562 0.251 283.7)`).
- **Content** (Ant Design): 14px text on a 22px line, 32px controls, 6px control corners and 8px cards and popups, `#f0f0f0` splits and `#d9d9d9` field borders, a `#fafafa` table header, plain (untinted) greys, and text at Ant's `rgba(0,0,0,.88)` / `.65`.
- **Shell** (Proton): a warm-grey `#f5f4f2` sidebar and header (`#16141c` Carbon in dark mode) around the white content panel, exposed as the `--onu-shell*` tokens.
- **Elevation**: borders and tonal surfaces; only popups (menus, selects, popovers, dialogs) cast a subtle shadow.
- **Dark mode**: Ant's dark algorithm for content (`#1f1f1f` surfaces, `#303030` / `#424242` borders, `#141414` layout grey).

Everything below is a token, so a project can move away from any of it.

# One variable for the brand colour

Set `--onu-primary` to any CSS colour and the whole library follows: buttons, focus rings, links, checked controls, the active sidebar item, tab ink bars, selected table rows, the current page, today and selected dates, and the first chart colour.

```css
:root {
    --onu-primary: oklch(0.55 0.15 240);
}
```

Hover and active shades and the text colour on top of primary are worked out from it in CSS. Text on primary switches between black and white automatically for contrast (in browsers with relative colour syntax; elsewhere it stays white). Override it with `--onu-primary-foreground` if your brand needs a specific colour.

In dark mode the primary colour is lifted so it keeps its contrast on dark backgrounds. Set `--onu-primary-dark` to choose the dark-mode shade yourself.

## Colour steps

Like Ant Design's palette, eight steps are derived from the primary colour with `color-mix(in oklab, …)`. Use them as `bg-primary-1`, `border-primary-3`, `text-primary-7` and so on.

| Step | Light | Dark | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--primary-1` (= `--primary-subtle`) | 10% primary on the background | 16% | Selected rows, selected options, tinted tags, filter chips, the bulk bar, pressed toggles |
| `--primary-2` | 22% | 26% | Hovered selected rows |
| `--primary-3` | 40% | 42% | Borders of tinted surfaces |
| `--primary-4`, `--primary-5` | 60%, 80% | 60%, 80% | Hovered field and default-button borders (5) |
| `--primary-6` | primary | primary | Fills, ink bars, focus |
| `--primary-7` | 14% darker | 20% lighter | Link and hovered-button text; active (pressed) fills in light mode |
| `--primary-8` (= `--primary-subtle-foreground` in light mode) | 30% darker | 38% lighter | Text on tinted surfaces |

# Brand tint

Onu's neutrals can be mixed with a small amount of the primary colour in CSS (`color-mix(in oklab, …)`), the way Radix Themes tints its grey scale. It is **off by default** (`--onu-tint: 0%`), which gives Ant Design's plain greys. Turn it on and these follow `--onu-primary`:

| Token | Used for | Primary mixed in (light / dark) |
|---|---|---|
| `--onu-accent`, `--onu-accent-foreground` | Hovered and highlighted menu, command, select and calendar items; ghost and outline button hovers; pressed toggles | 10% / 16%, text 30% / 15% |
| `--onu-secondary`, `--onu-secondary-foreground` | Secondary buttons and badges (tab counts) | 7% / 10%, text 20% / 10% |
| `--onu-muted`, `--onu-muted-foreground` | Muted surfaces and secondary text | 2% / 6%, text 10% / 8% |
| `--onu-border`, `--onu-input` | Borders and input outlines | 6% / 4%, inputs 10% / 6% |
| `--onu-sidebar`, `--onu-sidebar-accent`, `--onu-sidebar-accent-foreground`, `--onu-sidebar-border` | The app sidebar background, its hovers and border | 3% / 4%, hover 10% / 16% |

The amounts are kept small so text keeps WCAG AA contrast with any reasonable brand colour; dark surfaces take a little more so the tint still shows.

Set the strength with `--onu-tint` (a percentage of the amounts above; the default is `0%`, from `tokens.json`), on the root or on any element. The `data-onu-tint="none"` attribute turns it off again for part of a page:

```css
:root {
    --onu-tint: 100%; /* the full brand tint; 50% for half */
}
```

```html
<html data-onu-tint="none">
```

Setting a token yourself replaces the tinted value. The neutral starting points are available as `--onu-neutral-<token>` (for example `--onu-neutral-accent`), which is handy for keeping one token grey:

```css
:root {
    --onu-border: var(--onu-neutral-border);
}
```

A token you set on `:root` applies in dark mode too; set it again inside `.dark` for a different dark value.

# Granular tokens

Every token is a CSS variable you can set. The names follow shadcn/ui, prefixed with `--onu-`.

| Group | Tokens |
|---|---|
| Surfaces | `--onu-background`, `--onu-foreground`, `--onu-card`, `--onu-card-foreground`, `--onu-popover`, `--onu-popover-foreground` |
| Neutral | `--onu-secondary`, `--onu-muted`, `--onu-muted-foreground`, `--onu-accent`, `--onu-accent-foreground`, `--onu-border`, `--onu-input`, `--onu-ring` |
| Status | `--onu-destructive`, `--onu-success`, `--onu-warning`, `--onu-info` (each with `-foreground`) |
| Charts | `--onu-chart-1` … `--onu-chart-8` (`--onu-chart-1` defaults to primary) |
| Sidebar | `--onu-sidebar`, `--onu-sidebar-foreground`, `--onu-sidebar-primary`, `--onu-sidebar-accent`, `--onu-sidebar-border` |
| App shell | `--onu-shell`, `--onu-shell-foreground`, `--onu-shell-border`, `--onu-shell-field`, `--onu-shell-hover`, `--onu-shell-active`, `--onu-shell-weak` (see [App shell tokens](#app-shell-tokens)) |
| Layout grey | `--onu-layout` (Ant's `colorBgLayout`: the grey page behind dashboard cards) |
| Preset colours | `--onu-preset-{blue,cyan,green,red,gold}` with `-border` and `-foreground` (see [Preset colours](#preset-colours)) |
| Elevation | `--onu-shadow-popup` (the one shadow: menus, selects, popovers, dialogs) |
| Shape | `--onu-radius` (every radius derives from it; `0` gives square corners) |
| Type | `--onu-font-sans`, `--onu-font-thaana`, `--onu-font-thaana-bold`, `--onu-font-mono`, `--onu-font-serif`, `--onu-font-size` (body, 14px), `--onu-line-height` (1.5714, 22px) |
| Layout | `--onu-label-width`, `--onu-touch-target` |

Charts draw areas and bars with a soft gradient in these colours by default, so they rebrand with the theme too. Use `<ChartStyleProvider gradient={false}>` (from `@javaabu/onu/charts`) or a chart's `gradient={false}` for flat fills; see [BarChart](../charts/bar-chart.md#gradient-fills).

In Tailwind, use them as `bg-primary`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border-border`, `bg-success`, `fill-chart-3`, `bg-shell`, `bg-layout`, `bg-preset-green`, `shadow-popup`, `rounded-lg`, `font-thaana`, and so on.

## Shape

`--onu-radius` defaults to `0.375rem` (6px). The radius utilities derive from it: `rounded-sm` ≈ 4px (tags, menu items), `rounded-md` ≈ 5px, `rounded-lg` 6px (buttons, fields), `rounded-xl` 8px (cards, popups, dialogs).

## Type

Body text is 14px on a 22px line (`--onu-font-size`, `--onu-line-height`), Ant Design's base size; `text-sm` uses the same 22px line. Dhivehi text keeps its taller 1.75 line height. The `touch` density raises the body size to 16px.

## App shell tokens

The `--onu-shell*` tokens describe the area around the content panel (Proton's sidebar and header). Layout components use them; use them yourself as `bg-shell`, `text-shell-foreground`, `border-shell-border`, `bg-shell-field`, `hover:bg-shell-hover`, `bg-shell-active` and `bg-shell-weak`.

| Token | Light | Dark | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--onu-shell` | `#f5f4f2` | `#16141c` | Sidebar and header background |
| `--onu-shell-foreground` | `#1f1f1f` | `#ffffff` | Text on the shell |
| `--onu-shell-border` | `#e5e3e0` | `#343140` | Lines on the shell, the content panel's edge |
| `--onu-shell-field` | `#ffffff` | `#292733` | Fields on the shell (the header search) |
| `--onu-shell-hover` | `rgb(194 193 192 / 20%)` | `rgb(91 87 107 / 20%)` | Hovered nav items and header buttons |
| `--onu-shell-active` | `rgb(194 192 190 / 35%)` | `rgb(91 87 107 / 40%)` | The current nav item |
| `--onu-shell-weak` | `#eae7e4` | `#3f3b4c` | Weak fills on the shell: usage-meter tracks, avatar tiles |

## Preset colours

Ant Design's preset colours, for tags and status badges: a tinted fill, a matching border and a text shade with AA contrast on that fill, in light and dark mode. [StatusBadge](../display-and-feedback/status-badge.md) maps its tones to them (info blue, pending cyan, success green, danger red, warning gold), and [Tag](../display-and-feedback/tag.md) takes them as `color`.

| Token | Light (fill / border / text) | Dark (fill / border / text) |
|---|---|---|
| `--onu-preset-blue` | `#e6f4ff` / `#91caff` / `#0958d9` | `#111a2c` / `#15325b` / `#65a9f3` |
| `--onu-preset-cyan` | `#e6fffb` / `#87e8de` / `#006d75` | `#112123` / `#144848` / `#33bcb7` |
| `--onu-preset-green` | `#f6ffed` / `#b7eb8f` / `#237804` | `#162312` / `#274916` / `#6abe39` |
| `--onu-preset-red` | `#fff1f0` / `#ffa39e` / `#a8071a` | `#2a1215` / `#58181c` / `#f37370` |
| `--onu-preset-gold` | `#fffbe6` / `#ffe58f` / `#874d00` | `#2b2111` / `#594214` / `#e8b339` |

Each has `-border` and `-foreground` variants, e.g. `--onu-preset-green-border`.

# App shell and page layout

The default app layout is Proton Mail's shell around Ant Design's content: [`AppLayout`](../layout-and-navigation/app-layout.md) paints the sidebar, the header and the frame on the **shell colour** and the page on a white panel with a rounded top-start corner; [`PageTitle`](../layout-and-navigation/page-title.md) is Ant's PageHeader band, [`ListingPage`](../listing-pages/listing-page.md) the ProTable card layout and [`StatTile`](../charts/stat-tile.md) the ChartCard.

The shell reads these semantic tokens. Onu's theme defines them from the `--onu-shell*` and `--onu-layout` tokens (see [App shell tokens](#app-shell-tokens)); the components also carry Proton's values as fallbacks:

| Token | Used for | Fallback (light / dark) |
|---|---|---|
| `--shell`, `--shell-foreground` | Sidebar, header and frame; text on them | `#f5f4f2` / `#16141c`; `--foreground` |
| `--shell-border` | The panel's top and start line, the quota meter line | `#e5e3e0` / `#343140` |
| `--shell-field` | The header search field | `#ffffff` / `#292733` |
| `--shell-hover`, `--shell-active` | Sidebar items and header buttons | warm greys at 20% / 35% (light), Carbon greys at 20% / 40% (dark) |
| `--shell-weak` | The quota track, the account avatar tile | `#eae7e4` / `#3f3b4c` |
| `--layout` | The panel with `background="layout"` (dashboards of cards) | `#f5f5f5` / `#141414` |

For the previous look, use `<AppLayout variant="flat">`: the content fills the body, the header is bordered and the sidebar keeps the `--onu-sidebar` colours.

# Scoped themes

To theme part of a page, set tokens on an element together with the `data-onu-theme` attribute, so the derived colours are worked out again there:

```html
<section data-onu-theme style="--onu-primary: oklch(0.63 0.19 32)">
    …
</section>
```

# Tokens file

The defaults live in [`tokens.json`](https://github.com/Javaabu/onu/blob/main/tokens.json) (W3C Design Tokens format). It generates Onu's CSS and the Figma Variables in the Onu Figma kit, so design and code stay in step.

---

<!-- docs/guides/dark-mode.md -->

# Dark mode

Every Onu component has a dark variant. Dark mode turns on when an ancestor has the `dark` class or `data-theme="dark"`, so it works with any toggling approach.

`ThemeProvider` handles it for you: light, dark or following the system, remembered in `localStorage`.

```tsx
import { ThemeProvider, ThemeToggle, useTheme } from '@javaabu/onu';

<ThemeProvider defaultTheme="system">
    <App />
</ThemeProvider>

function MyToggle() {
    const { theme, resolvedTheme, setTheme } = useTheme();
    return <button onClick={() => setTheme(resolvedTheme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark')}>Toggle</button>;
}
```

| Prop | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `defaultTheme` | `"system"` | Theme when nothing is stored |
| `forcedTheme` | | Fix the theme, e.g. `"light"` for print pages |
| `storageKey` | `"onu-theme"` | `localStorage` key |

The provider sets `class="dark"`, `data-theme` and `color-scheme` on `<html>`, so dialogs and menus in portals follow it.

In server-rendered apps, add `themeScript()` to `<head>` to apply the stored theme before the page paints:

```tsx
<script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: themeScript() }} />
```

In your own styles use Tailwind's `dark:` variant, which Onu configures for both the class and the attribute.

---

<!-- docs/guides/rtl.md -->

# RTL

Every Onu component works right-to-left with no extra props.

# Setting the direction

`OnuProvider` takes the direction from the locale (`dv` is RTL) and sets `dir` on `<html>`, so overlays in portals follow it too. Override it with `dir`:

```tsx
<OnuProvider locale="dv">…</OnuProvider>          // RTL
<OnuProvider locale="en" dir="rtl">…</OnuProvider> // RTL with English strings
```

# What changes in RTL

- Layout uses logical properties: start/end instead of left/right.
- Directional icons (arrows, chevrons, back/next, undo/redo, send) mirror; others (play, check, logos) do not.
- Arrow keys follow the visual order in tabs, menus, sliders, carousels and calendars.
- Sliders, progress bars, carousels, steppers, timelines, pagination and time axes run right to left.
- Sidebars and sheets use `side="start" | "end"`, which flips with the direction.

Inputs for Latin-only data (email, URL, phone, numbers, codes, OTP) stay left-to-right inside an RTL page. Free text uses `dir="auto"`, and Thaana fields are RTL.

# Writing your own components

Use Tailwind's logical utilities: `ms-*`/`me-*`, `ps-*`/`pe-*`, `start-*`/`end-*`, `text-start`/`text-end`, `rounded-s-*`/`rounded-e-*`, `border-s`/`border-e`. Onu's ESLint config rejects physical `left`/`right` utilities. For the rare transform that must flip, use the `rtl:` variant: `rtl:-scale-x-100`.

Read the direction with `useDirection()`.

---

<!-- docs/guides/dhivehi-and-locales.md -->

# Dhivehi & locales

Onu ships with English (`en`) and Dhivehi (`dv`). Every built-in string — button labels, placeholders, screen-reader text, pagination, date pickers — comes from the active locale.

```tsx
import { dv } from '@javaabu/onu/locales/dv';

<OnuProvider locale={dv}>…</OnuProvider>
```

# Loading Dhivehi

Only apps that use Dhivehi download its text (about 15 kB brotli):

- `locale={dv}`, with `dv` imported from `@javaabu/onu/locales/dv`, bundles Dhivehi with your app. The first render is already in Dhivehi. Use this when Dhivehi is the main or a common language.
- `locale="dv"` loads Dhivehi on demand, as a separate chunk, when the provider first needs it. Direction and `lang` switch at once, and strings show in English until the chunk arrives (usually within the first frames). This suits a language switcher in a mostly English app.
- English needs nothing: leave out `locale` (or pass `"en"`). Each component brings the English text it uses, so a page with a text field does not carry the strings of the data table, the map or the editor.

`import { dv } from '@javaabu/onu'` still works too; it bundles Dhivehi like the `locales/dv` import.

# Overriding strings

```tsx
<OnuProvider
    locale="dv"
    messages={{ common: { save: 'ރައްކާކުރޭ' }, listing: { selected: '{count} ޚިޔާރުކުރެވިފައި' } }}
>
```

Use `useTranslation()` for your own components:

```tsx
const { t } = useTranslation();
t('common.save');
t('listing.showing', { from: 26, to: 50, total: 312 });
```

In English, `t()` finds Onu's strings in the components your app has loaded. If your own code uses a key from a namespace none of your components use (say `t('map.zoomIn')` without any map component), pass the full English set, `<OnuProvider locale={en}>` with `en` from `@javaabu/onu`, or add the string with `messages`.

Messages support `{param}` interpolation and plural forms (`{ one: '…', other: '…' }` chosen from the `count` param).

# Adding a locale

A locale is an object. Missing strings fall back to English, and `dateFns` can be left out for English month and weekday names:

```ts
import { en, type OnuLocale } from '@javaabu/onu';
import { ar } from 'date-fns/locale/ar';

const arabic: OnuLocale = {
    code: 'ar',
    name: 'العربية',
    dir: 'rtl',
    messages: { ...en.messages /* translated */ },
    dateFns: ar,
    weekStartsOn: 6,
    numberLocale: 'ar',
    hourCycle: 12,
};
```

# Dates and numbers

- Dhivehi month and weekday names, AM/PM (މކ / މފ) and relative times ("2 ދުވަސް ކުރިން") come from Onu's Dhivehi date-fns locale (`dvDateFns`), since date-fns and browsers have no Dhivehi data.
- Numbers use Western digits, as is standard in the Maldives.
- Hijri dates use the Umm al-Qura calendar (see the Hijri date component).
- Sorting and search use `Intl.Collator`, so Thaana sorts correctly.

## Formatting dates, numbers and amounts yourself

Three hooks format values the way Onu's components do, with the active locale. Use them for your own text (table cells, cards, summaries) so it matches the components and switches with the locale.

```tsx
import { useFormatCurrency, useFormatDate, useFormatNumber } from "@javaabu/onu"

function ApplicationSummary({ application }) {
  const formatDate = useFormatDate()
  const formatNumber = useFormatNumber()
  const formatCurrency = useFormatCurrency()
  return (
    <p>
      {formatDate(application.submitted_at)} {/* "Mar 12, 2026" · "12 މާރޗް 2026" */}
      {formatDate(application.submitted_at, "EEEE d MMMM")} {/* any date-fns pattern */}
      {formatNumber(application.pages)} {/* "1,234" (Western digits in Dhivehi too) */}
      {formatCurrency(application.fee)} {/* "MVR 1,250.00" · "ރ. 1,250.00" */}
    </p>
  )
}
```

| Hook                  | Returns                                                                                                   |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `useFormatDate()`     | `(date, pattern = "PP") => string`. `date` is a `Date`, timestamp or ISO string; invalid or empty gives `""`. Uses the locale's date-fns locale (`dvDateFns` for Dhivehi) and week start. |
| `useFormatNumber()`   | `(value, options?) => string` with `Intl.NumberFormat` options and the locale's `numberLocale`.            |
| `useFormatCurrency()` | `(value, { decimals = 2, compact = false }?) => string` in Maldivian Rufiyaa, worded by the `common.currency` string (`"MVR {amount}"`, `"ރ. {amount}"`). The amount is wrapped in Unicode isolates so it keeps its order next to Thaana. |

Charts have their own `useChartFormat` in `@javaabu/onu/charts`, with axis and percentage helpers.

# Fonts

Dhivehi text uses Faruma, with MV Faseyha for headings and bold, both bundled with `fonts.css`. See [Fonts](./fonts.md).

---

<!-- docs/guides/thaana-input.md -->

# Thaana input

Onu can type Thaana from a Latin keyboard, so users don't need a Dhivehi keyboard installed. It is a React version of [JTK](https://github.com/jawish/jtk) (Javascript Thaana Keyboard) and uses the same keyboard layouts.

# On components

Every component that accepts free text has a `thaana` prop: text inputs, textareas, search boxes, autocomplete, tags, searchable selects, inline edit, the command palette, comment and note composers, the translations editor and the rich text editors.

```tsx
<TextInput thaana />
<TextInput thaana thaanaToggle />   // with a Thaana/Latin button
<ThaanaInput />                     // Thaana on and toggle shown by default
<Textarea thaana={{ keymap: 'typewriter', paste: 'transliterate' }} />
```

With Thaana on, the field is right-to-left, `lang="dv"`, and uses the Thaana font. Users switch between Thaana and Latin with the toggle button or <kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>T</kbd>; screen readers hear "Thaana typing on/off".

Inputs that must hold Latin text (email, password, URL, numbers, phone, OTP, slug, colour) do not offer it.

# Keyboard layouts

| `keymap` | Layout |
|---|---|
| `phonetic` (default) | Phonetic (Segha version), the most common layout |
| `phonetic-hh` | Phonetic (Hassan Hameed version): different alifu, abafili, aabaafili, gaafu and sukun |
| `typewriter` | The standard Thaana typewriter layout |

Pass your own map with `createKeymap(latinKeys, thaanaCharacters)`.

# Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `keymap` | `"phonetic"` | Layout name or a custom keymap |
| `paste` | `"keep"` | `"transliterate"` converts pasted Latin text to Thaana |
| `toggleShortcut` | Alt+Shift+T | `{ code, altKey, shiftKey, ctrlKey, metaKey }`, or `false` |
| `defaultEnabled` | `true` | Start in Thaana mode |

# On your own elements

```tsx
import { useThaanaInput, attachThaanaKeyboard, transliterate } from '@javaabu/onu/thaana';

function MyField() {
    const ref = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
    const { enabled, toggle } = useThaanaInput(ref, { keymap: 'phonetic' });
    return <input ref={ref} dir={enabled ? 'rtl' : 'auto'} lang="dv" />;
}

// Without React
const keyboard = attachThaanaKeyboard(document.querySelector('#name'));
keyboard.setEnabled(false);
keyboard.detach();

transliterate('dhivehi'); // "ދހިވެހި"
```

# How it works

- Typed characters are converted in the `beforeinput` event, so it works with physical keyboards and on-screen keyboards that send characters directly — including Android, where key codes are not available.
- Predictive keyboards (such as Gboard) that compose whole words are converted when the word is finished.
- If the user already types with a Thaana keyboard or another input method, their text passes through untouched.
- <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>⌘</kbd> shortcuts are never intercepted.
- Text is inserted so the browser's undo still works.
- It works on inputs, textareas and `contenteditable` elements; the editors use a Tiptap extension built on the same keymaps.

---

<!-- docs/guides/icons.md -->

# Icons

Onu uses [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) icons by default, with no setup. Components ask for icons by **semantic name** (`close`, `search`, `chevron-down`, …), so you can switch every built-in icon to another set — such as FontAwesome Pro — in one place.

```tsx
import { Icon } from '@javaabu/onu';

<Icon name="search" />                     // decorative (hidden from screen readers)
<Icon name="trash" label="Delete" />       // meaningful: role="img" + label
<Icon name="calendar" size="lg" className="text-primary" />
```

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `name` | Semantic icon name (see `SEMANTIC_ICON_NAMES`) |
| `label` | Accessible name. Without it the icon is decorative |
| `size` | `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` or a number of pixels |
| `flip` | Force RTL mirroring on/off (on by default for directional icons) |
| `fallback` | Icon component or element used when no icon set has `name` |

# How names are resolved

`<Icon name="…">` looks for the name in this order:

1. your overrides from `OnuProvider icons={…}`
2. the default Lucide set (`lucideIconMap`), which `OnuProvider` loads on demand
3. the `fallback` prop
4. a generic alert icon

Neither Onu's components nor `OnuProvider` import the default set, so a page that uses only a few components does not ship all ~250 default icons. For example, importing just `Button` is about 12 kB (brotli) rather than 21 kB, and `OnuProvider` about 1 kB. Components that always show the same glyph, such as `Spinner`, a button's loading spinner, dialog close buttons and menu chevrons, pass that Lucide icon as `fallback`. They work even outside `OnuProvider`, and your `icons` overrides still replace them.

The first time an icon is chosen by name at runtime, such as `<Button startIcon="add">` or a navigation item's `icon: "home"`, `OnuProvider` loads the default set as a separate chunk (about 9 kB brotli). Until it arrives, which is usually within the first frames, the icon renders as an empty placeholder of the same size, so nothing shifts. Apps that never choose icons by name never download it.

To have every name resolved on the first render (for example in server-rendered pages or screenshots), bundle the set up front by passing it as overrides:

```tsx
import { lucideIconMap, OnuProvider } from '@javaabu/onu';

<OnuProvider icons={lucideIconMap}>            // or { ...lucideIconMap, add: MyAddIcon }
```

Wrap your app in `OnuProvider` (see [Installation](../installation-and-setup.md)). Outside it, icons chosen by name at runtime fall back to the generic icon. The `Icon` you import from `@javaabu/onu` is the exception: it includes the default set, so it resolves every name anywhere.

# FontAwesome Pro

Install FontAwesome's core packages and your Pro icon packages (they need your FontAwesome licence token for `npm.fontawesome.com`). Onu never bundles Pro icons.

```bash
npm install @fortawesome/fontawesome-svg-core @fortawesome/react-fontawesome @fortawesome/pro-regular-svg-icons
```

Then switch every built-in icon:

```tsx
import { fontAwesomeIconMap, requiredFontAwesomeIcons } from '@javaabu/onu/icons/fontawesome';
import { far } from '@fortawesome/pro-regular-svg-icons';

<OnuProvider icons={fontAwesomeIconMap({ style: 'regular', icons: [far] })}>
```

Importing the whole pack is simplest. To keep bundles small, import only the icons Onu uses — `requiredFontAwesomeIcons()` lists their names — or register them with `library.add` yourself.

Styles: `solid`, `regular`, `light`, `thin`, `duotone`, `sharp-solid`, `sharp-regular`, `sharp-light`, `sharp-thin`, `sharp-duotone-solid`, or any prefix (for example a Kit's `fak`). Icons missing in the chosen style fall back to `fallbackStyle` (solid). Duotone icons pick up the theme: the secondary layer uses the primary colour.

FontAwesome Free works the same way with `@fortawesome/free-solid-svg-icons`.

# Iconify (200,000+ icons)

```tsx
import { iconifySource, iconifyIconMap, registerIconifyCollections } from '@javaabu/onu/icons/iconify';
import tabler from '@iconify-json/tabler/icons.json';

const iconify = iconifySource({ collections: [tabler] });

<OnuProvider iconSources={[iconify]}>
```

Iconify runs offline: only the collections you register are used, and no requests go to the Iconify API — so it works on kiosks, intranets and under a strict Content Security Policy.

# Stored icon ids

`DynamicIcon` renders icons saved as strings (for example from a CMS or the menu builder): `lucide:house`, `tabler:home`, `fa:regular:house`. The icon picker returns ids in this format.

```tsx
<DynamicIcon id={menuItem.icon} />
```

# RTL

Directional icons — arrows, chevrons, back/forward, undo/redo, reply, send, log in/out, external link — mirror automatically in RTL, whichever icon set you use.

---

<!-- docs/guides/fonts.md -->

# Fonts

Onu's optional font pack. Install the three Latin and fallback fonts it loads from npm, then import it after `tailwind.css`:

```bash
npm install @fontsource-variable/inter @fontsource-variable/jetbrains-mono @fontsource-variable/noto-sans-thaana
```

```css
@import "@javaabu/onu/fonts.css";
```

`fonts.css` imports these packages, so without them the CSS build fails with "Can't resolve '@fontsource-variable/inter'". Faruma and MV Faseyha need nothing extra: they ship inside `@javaabu/onu`.

| Role | Font | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Interface | Inter | `@fontsource-variable/inter` |
| Thaana text | **Faruma** | bundled with Onu |
| Thaana headings and bold | **MV Faseyha** | bundled with Onu |
| Thaana fallback | Noto Sans Thaana | `@fontsource-variable/noto-sans-thaana` |
| Code, IDs, keys | JetBrains Mono | `@fontsource-variable/jetbrains-mono` |

Optional presets in `@javaabu/onu/fonts-optional.css`: Geist (set `data-font="geist"` on an element) and Source Serif 4 for long-form reading (`font-serif`). It needs `npm install @fontsource-variable/geist @fontsource-variable/source-serif-4`.

All of these are self-hosted from npm, so no requests go to a font CDN.

# Thaana fonts

Onu ships Faruma and MV Faseyha with `fonts.css`, as `woff2` files subset to Thaana and its punctuation (about 12 kB each). Their `unicode-range` means a browser only downloads them when a page shows Thaana text, and Latin text in a mixed sentence stays in Inter.

- **Faruma** is used for Dhivehi body text (`--onu-font-thaana`).
- **MV Faseyha** is used for Dhivehi headings and `<b>`/`<strong>` (`--onu-font-thaana-bold`). Both fonts have a single weight and Onu turns off faux bold for Dhivehi, so emphasis uses the second face instead.
- Characters neither font covers fall back to Noto Sans Thaana.

If you don't import `fonts.css`, the same names still apply to copies installed on the device.

# Mixed Dhivehi and English

Font stacks list a Latin font and then a Thaana font. Because each font only covers its own script, a sentence that mixes Dhivehi and English uses the right font for each part automatically.

# Your own fonts

```css
:root {
    --onu-font-sans: "My Sans", Faruma, sans-serif;
    --onu-font-thaana: "My Thaana", Faruma, sans-serif;
    --onu-font-thaana-bold: "My Thaana Bold", "MV Faseyha", sans-serif;
}
```

Numbers in tables, stat tiles, pagination and timers use tabular figures so they line up.

---

<!-- docs/guides/accessibility.md -->

# Accessibility

Onu targets **WCAG 2.2 Level AA** for every component, in light and dark mode and in both directions.

What you get out of the box:

- Widgets follow the [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/) (built on Radix and React Aria primitives).
- Everything works with the keyboard, with a visible focus ring that is never hidden behind sticky bars.
- Dialogs, sheets and menus trap focus while open and return it to whatever opened them.
- Form fields link labels, help text and errors (`aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`); errors and async results are announced in live regions.
- Targets are at least 24×24px, and at least 44×44px on touch screens.
- Colour is never the only signal: statuses, validation and chart series also use icons, text or patterns.
- Animations are turned off for users who prefer reduced motion.
- Charts and maps have text alternatives (data tables, marker lists, coordinates).
- `lang` is set on Dhivehi and English content so screen readers switch voice.

What you still need to do:

- Give every control a label (a `FormField`, a `<label>`, or `aria-label`).
- Give meaningful icons a `label`, and images real `alt` text.
- Add a [`SkipLink`](../layout-and-navigation/skip-link.md) at the top of each layout.
- Keep your own colours to the token palette, or check their contrast.

Each component's docs page lists its keyboard interactions. Onu's tests run [axe](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) on every component, and the web app is scanned in CI.

---

<!-- docs/guides/style-overrides.md -->

# Style overrides

Every component can be restyled without forking it.

# `className`

Classes you pass are merged with the component's own using [tailwind-merge](https://github.com/dcastil/tailwind-merge), so yours win:

```tsx
<Button className="rounded-full px-6">Save</Button>
```

# `classNames` for parts

Compound components take a `classNames` object with one entry per part:

```tsx
<FormField label="Name" classNames={{ label: 'font-semibold', help: 'italic' }}>…</FormField>
<TextInput startAddon="@" classNames={{ root: 'bg-muted', input: 'font-mono' }} />
```

# Variants

Variants are built with [class-variance-authority](https://cva.style) and exported, so you can reuse them on other elements:

```tsx
import { buttonVariants } from '@javaabu/onu';

<a className={buttonVariants({ variant: 'outline', size: 'sm' })} href="/export">Export</a>
```

# `asChild`

Buttons, links and triggers accept `asChild` to render your own element with their styles and behaviour:

```tsx
<Button asChild>
    <Link href="/users/create">New user</Link>
</Button>
```

# Data attributes

Components expose `data-slot` (which part), plus `data-state`, `data-variant`, `data-size`, `data-invalid` and similar attributes for styling from CSS:

```css
[data-slot="form-field"][data-invalid] [data-slot="label"] { text-decoration: underline; }
```

# Primitives

The shadcn/ui primitives Onu builds on are available from `@javaabu/onu/primitives` when you need to compose something new.

Onu never uses `!important`, and inline styles only for values that change at runtime (positions, progress).

---

<!-- docs/guides/forms-and-laravel.md -->

# Forms & Laravel validation

Onu's form components are built around Laravel's conventions, so server validation errors show up under the right fields with no glue code.

# Fields

Wrap every control in a [`FormField`](../form-scaffolding/form-field.md). Give it the input's `name` (bracket notation is fine) and it wires the label, help text, errors and ARIA attributes:

```tsx
<FormField label="Name" name="name" required help="As shown on your ID card">
    <TextInput thaana />
</FormField>
```

Labels are stacked by default. Use `labelLayout="inline"` on a field, a [`Form`](../form-scaffolding/form.md), a `FormLayoutProvider` or `OnuProvider` to put labels beside the controls; they stack again in narrow containers.

# Validation errors

Laravel returns validation errors as a 422 response:

```json
{
    "message": "The email has already been taken.",
    "errors": { "email": ["The email has already been taken."], "items.0.name": ["The name field is required."] }
}
```

[`Form`](../form-scaffolding/form.md) understands this shape wherever it comes from — the thrown body, an axios error, a fetch `Response`, or Inertia's `errors` prop — and then:

1. shows each message under its field (`items[0][name]` matches `items.0.name`);
2. focuses the first invalid field, opening collapsed sections if needed;
3. shows an [error summary](../form-scaffolding/validation-summary.md) with links to every field.

```tsx
<Form onSubmit={(values) => axios.post('/applications', values)}>
    …
    <SubmitButton>Submit</SubmitButton>
</Form>
```

Without `Form`, provide errors to a section with `FormErrorsProvider`.

# Inertia

```tsx
import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/react';

const form = useForm({ name: '', email: '' });

<Form onSubmit={() => form.post('/users')} errors={form.errors} processing={form.processing}>
    <FormField label="Name" name="name">
        <TextInput value={form.data.name} onChange={(e) => form.setData('name', e.target.value)} />
    </FormField>
    <SubmitButton>Save</SubmitButton>
</Form>
```

# Plain HTML forms

Every input renders a real form field with a Laravel-friendly `name`, so a normal `<form method="post">` submits what Laravel expects:

| Component | Submitted as |
|---|---|
| Date picker | `due_date=2026-03-12` |
| Date range | `period[from]`, `period[to]` |
| Multi-select, tags | `tags[]` |
| Map picker | `location[lat]`, `location[lng]` |
| Repeating group | `items[0][name]`, `items[1][name]` |
| Rich text editor | HTML in a hidden input (`""` when empty, so `required` works) |
| Custom attribute fields | `attributes[key]`, booleans as `1`/`0` |

# Unsaved changes and the save bar

On edit pages, the [`SaveBar`](../form-scaffolding/save-bar.md) lists each change in plain words, keeps Save disabled until something changed, offers Discard, and warns before leaving with unsaved changes ([`useUnsavedChangesGuard`](../form-scaffolding/unsaved-changes-guard.md)).

# API-backed selects

[`ApiSelect`](../choice-inputs/api-select.md) reads Laravel API resources and paginators with no configuration: it sends `search`, `page` and `per_page`, reads `data`, and loads the next page as the list scrolls.

```tsx
<FormField label="Island" name="island_id">
    <ApiSelect url="/api/islands" />
</FormField>
```

# Uploads

[`InstantFileUpload`](../files-and-media/instant-file-upload.md) uploads as soon as a file is chosen, sends your CSRF header, shows progress, and reads 422 errors from the upload endpoint. The uploaded file's id goes into a hidden input for the main form.

---

<!-- docs/guides/inertia-and-nextjs.md -->

# Inertia & Next.js

Onu is plain React, so it works in Vite apps, Laravel + Inertia (React) and Next.js.

# Links

Components that render links (link buttons, breadcrumbs, side navigation, pagination, nav tabs, …) use the link component you give `OnuProvider`:

```tsx
// Inertia
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react';
<OnuProvider linkComponent={Link}>…</OnuProvider>

// Next.js
import Link from 'next/link';
<OnuProvider linkComponent={Link}>…</OnuProvider>
```

Or pass your own element to a single component with `asChild`.

# Laravel + Inertia

Wrap the app in `TooltipProvider` (a collapsed `AppSidebar` shows its labels as tooltips) and pass Inertia's `Link` as `linkComponent`. Inertia's `Link` types its `onClick` for any element rather than an anchor, so TypeScript needs a cast:

```tsx
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react';
import { OnuProvider, TooltipProvider, type LinkComponent } from '@javaabu/onu';

<OnuProvider locale={usePage().props.locale} linkComponent={Link as LinkComponent}>
    <TooltipProvider>…</TooltipProvider>
</OnuProvider>
```

Render `<html lang dir>` from the Blade root view so right-to-left pages are correct before React loads.

# Next.js App Router

Every Onu component file is marked `"use client"`, so Server Components can render Onu components directly, as long as every prop is serialisable (strings, numbers, elements). Anything that takes a function (`onSubmit`, `onChange`, `linkComponent`) belongs in a `"use client"` file.

Put `ThemeProvider`, `OnuProvider` and `TooltipProvider` in a client component, and render the layout's `<html lang dir>` on the server so right-to-left pages are correct in the first HTML:

```tsx
// components/providers.tsx
'use client';

import { OnuProvider, ThemeProvider, TooltipProvider } from '@javaabu/onu';
import Link from 'next/link';

export function Providers({ locale, children }) {
    return (
        <ThemeProvider>
            <OnuProvider locale={locale} linkComponent={Link}>
                <TooltipProvider>{children}</TooltipProvider>
            </OnuProvider>
        </ThemeProvider>
    );
}
```

Because the package is a client module, `themeScript()` can't be called from a Server Component. Render it from a small client component instead, which puts the script in the server-rendered HTML:

```tsx
// components/theme-script.tsx
'use client';

import { themeScript } from '@javaabu/onu';

export function ThemeScript() {
    return <script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: themeScript() }} suppressHydrationWarning />;
}
```

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx (a Server Component)
export default async function RootLayout({ children }) {
    const locale = (await cookies()).get('locale')?.value === 'dv' ? 'dv' : 'en';
    return (
        <html lang={locale} dir={locale === 'dv' ? 'rtl' : 'ltr'} suppressHydrationWarning>
            <head>
                <ThemeScript />
            </head>
            <body>
                <Providers locale={locale}>{children}</Providers>
            </body>
        </html>
    );
}
```

# Starter templates

The repository has two complete starters, built and tested in CI against the current library:

- [`templates/nextjs`](https://github.com/Javaabu/onu/tree/main/templates/nextjs): the setup above, a page of Onu components rendered by a Server Component, an English / Dhivehi switch, a form backed by a Server Action, and a check that the server-rendered HTML contains Onu's markup.
- [`templates/laravel-inertia-react`](https://github.com/Javaabu/onu/tree/main/templates/laravel-inertia-react): Laravel with Inertia, React and TypeScript, an `AppLayout` / `AppSidebar` admin shell, an English / Dhivehi switch stored in the session, and a form that shows Laravel's validation errors, with feature tests.

Each template's README shows how to copy it and use the npm package.

# Inertia validation errors

Inertia puts Laravel's validation errors in `usePage().props.errors`. Pass them to `FormErrorsProvider` (or `Form`'s `errors`) and every field with a matching `name` shows its message:

```tsx
const { errors } = usePage().props;

<FormErrorsProvider errors={errors}>
    <FormField label="Email" name="email">
        <TextInput />
    </FormField>
</FormErrorsProvider>
```

<!-- docs/guides/ai-assistants.md -->

# AI assistants

Onu's docs are written so AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, ChatGPT and others) can use them: every page is plain Markdown with a Props table and an Accessibility section, and there is a short list of [rules for writing Onu code](./rules-for-ai.md). Give your assistant the docs in one of these ways.

# Docs in the package

The npm package ships its docs, so they always match the version you have installed:

| File | What |
| --- | --- |
| `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/llms.txt` | The rules, then every component, hook and guide with one line on what it is for and the path to its page |
| `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/docs/<group>/<name>.md` | One page, e.g. `docs/text-inputs/password-input.md` |
| `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/llms-full.txt` | Every page in one file (about 850 kB; for tools that index docs, not for a chat) |
| `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/docs/index.json` | The index as JSON |

Point your assistant at them from the project's instructions file (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/rules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`):

```md
## UI

This app uses Onu (@javaabu/onu) for all UI. Before writing UI code, read the Rules section of
node_modules/@javaabu/onu/llms.txt. Before using a component, read its page in
node_modules/@javaabu/onu/docs/ (paths are listed in llms.txt) and use only the props it lists.
```

# On the docs site

The site serves the same files at its root: [`/llms.txt`](https://onu.on-forge.com/llms.txt), [`/llms-full.txt`](https://onu.on-forge.com/llms-full.txt) and `/docs/<group>/<name>.md`. Each component page has a **Copy page** button that copies the page as Markdown, with a menu to view the Markdown or open the page in Claude or ChatGPT.

`llms.txt` on the site also lists the sample pages (whole screens such as sign in, listing and settings pages) with links to their source.

# MCP server

`@javaabu/onu-mcp` is a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server for assistants that support MCP. It reads the docs of the `@javaabu/onu` installed in your project (from the folder the assistant runs in, or a parent folder), and falls back to the docs it was published with.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `onu_get_rules` | The rules for writing Onu code |
| `onu_list_components` | Every page by section, with a one-line description; `section` lists one |
| `onu_get_doc` | A page as Markdown, by component name (`PasswordInput`), file name or path |
| `onu_search_docs` | Searches every page, e.g. `"date range laravel"` |

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope project --transport stdio onu -- npx -y @javaabu/onu-mcp
```

Other clients (Cursor's `.cursor/mcp.json`, VS Code's `.vscode/mcp.json`, Claude Desktop):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "onu": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@javaabu/onu-mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Set `ONU_DOCS_DIR` to read the docs from another folder.

# Claude Code plugin

The Onu repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. The `onu` plugin adds a skill that tells Claude to load the rules and read each component's page before using it, and sets up the MCP server:

```text
/plugin marketplace add Javaabu/onu
/plugin install onu@javaabu-onu
```

<!-- docs/guides/rules-for-ai.md -->

# Rules for AI assistants

Short rules for AI coding assistants (and people) writing UI with Onu. They sit at the top of [`llms.txt`](./ai-assistants.md), and the Onu MCP server and Claude Code plugin hand them to the assistant before it writes code.

# Before writing code

- Look up a component's page before using it: `node_modules/@javaabu/onu/docs/<group>/<name>.md`, `onu_get_doc` in the MCP server, or the site's `llms.txt`. Each page has a **Props** table and an **Accessibility** section. Use only the props listed there.
- Prefer an Onu component over writing your own or using a shadcn/ui primitive directly. `llms.txt` lists every component with one line on what it is for. Only reach for `@javaabu/onu/primitives` (the shadcn/ui parts Onu is built on) to compose something Onu doesn't have.
- Don't add other UI kits (MUI, Chakra, Ant Design, Headless UI, a separate shadcn/ui copy) next to Onu.

# Setup

- One CSS entry: `@import "tailwindcss"; @import "@javaabu/onu/tailwind.css";` and, for the font pack, `@import "@javaabu/onu/fonts.css";`, which needs `npm install @fontsource-variable/inter @fontsource-variable/jetbrains-mono @fontsource-variable/noto-sans-thaana` first.
- Wrap the app once in `<ThemeProvider><OnuProvider>…</OnuProvider></ThemeProvider>`. `OnuProvider` sets `lang`, `dir` and density on `<html>`, so portals follow.
- Dhivehi: `locale={dv}` with `import { dv } from "@javaabu/onu/locales/dv"`, or `locale="dv"` to load it on demand. English needs no `locale`.
- Inertia or Next.js: pass the router's `Link` as `linkComponent` on `OnuProvider`; Onu's links and `href` props then use it.

# Imports

- Components, hooks and helpers come from `@javaabu/onu`. Heavy features have their own entry: `@javaabu/onu/charts`, `/maps`, `/editor`, `/calendar`, `/media`, `/query-builder`, `/export`, `/thaana`, `/icons/iconify`, `/icons/fontawesome`. The docs page's first code block shows the import.
- Never import from `@javaabu/onu/dist/...` or `@javaabu/onu/src/...`.

# Forms (Laravel)

- Put every control inside `FormField` with the field's `name` (bracket notation is fine, `items[0][name]`). `FormField` wires the label, help, errors and ARIA. Don't hand-write `<label>`, error text or `aria-describedby`.
- Use `Form` with an `onSubmit` that returns the request promise (axios, fetch or Inertia). It shows Laravel 422 errors under the fields, focuses the first one and shows the error summary. With Inertia, pass `errors={form.errors}` and `processing={form.processing}`.
- Submit with `SubmitButton` (spinner, no double submit), not a plain `Button type="submit"`.
- Pick the specific input: `EmailInput`, `PasswordInput`, `PhoneInput`, `NumberInput`, `DatePicker`, `ApiSelect` (Laravel paginated API), `InstantFileUpload`, and so on, rather than `TextInput type="…"`.
- Edit pages get `SaveBar`; index pages get `ListingPage` (or `DataTable` with `useListingState`).

# Dhivehi, Thaana and RTL

- Free-text fields that may hold Dhivehi take `thaana` (`<TextInput thaana />`, `<Textarea thaana />`), or use `ThaanaInput`. Never add `thaana` to email, password, URL, number, phone, OTP or code inputs; they stay LTR by design.
- Use logical Tailwind utilities only: `ms-*`/`me-*`, `ps-*`/`pe-*`, `start-*`/`end-*`, `text-start`/`text-end`, `border-s`/`border-e`, `rounded-s-*`/`rounded-e-*`. Never `ml-*`, `mr-*`, `pl-*`, `pr-*`, `left-*`, `right-*`, `text-left` or `text-right`. Flip transforms with `rtl:`.
- Sides are `side="start" | "end"`, not left/right.
- Format dates, numbers and money with `useFormatDate`, `useFormatNumber` and `useFormatCurrency` (MVR), not `toLocaleString` or hand-built strings. Numbers use Western digits in Dhivehi too.
- Built-in strings come from the locale. For your own strings use `useTranslation()` or your app's i18n, and override Onu's strings with `OnuProvider messages`.

# Styling and theming

- Brand colour: set `--onu-primary` (one variable re-themes everything). Use the theme tokens (`bg-background`, `text-foreground`, `bg-primary`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border`, `bg-card`, …), never fixed colours like `bg-blue-600` or hex values, so dark mode and themes keep working.
- Restyle with `className` (merged with tailwind-merge, yours wins) and `classNames={{ part: "…" }}` for parts. Reuse exported variants such as `buttonVariants`. Use `asChild` to render your own element. No `!important`, no inline styles for static values.
- Density (`compact` to `touch`) and dark mode come from the providers; don't hard-code heights or `dark:` colours on Onu components.

# Icons

- Use `<Icon name="search" />` and `startIcon="add"` / `endIcon="…"` props with semantic names, not imports from `lucide-react`. Give icons that carry meaning a `label`; icon-only buttons need an accessible name (`aria-label` or the component's `label` prop).
- Directional icons mirror in RTL on their own; don't flip them yourself.

# Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA)

- Onu components already handle roles, focus and keyboard. Don't remove focus rings, add `tabIndex` to non-interactive elements, or replace buttons with clickable `div`s.
- Announce async results with `toast()`, `announce()` or `LiveRegion`; hide text visually with `VisuallyHidden`, not `display: none`.
- Confirm destructive actions with `confirm()` / `useConfirm()` or the item's `confirm` option, not `window.confirm`.

# Bundle size

- Import only what you use; every entry is tree-shaken. Keep charts, maps, the editor, the calendar and media in their own entries (and lazy routes when they are big).

---

<!-- docs/accessibility/visually-hidden.md -->

# VisuallyHidden

Content for screen readers only. It is taken out of the visual layout with Tailwind's `sr-only` but is still read out, and focusable content inside it stays in the tab order. Use it for icon-button names, extra link context and headings that structure a page without being shown.

```tsx
import { VisuallyHidden } from "@javaabu/onu"

<Button variant="outline" size="icon">
  <Icon name="edit" />
  <VisuallyHidden>Edit application</VisuallyHidden>
</Button>

<a href="/fees">Read more<VisuallyHidden> about passport fees</VisuallyHidden></a>

// Your own element, e.g. a heading
<VisuallyHidden asChild>
  <h2>Search filters</h2>
</VisuallyHidden>

// A skip link that appears while it has focus
<VisuallyHidden focusable asChild>
  <a href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
</VisuallyHidden>
```

For a complete skip link with the right styling, use [`SkipLink`](../layout-and-navigation/skip-link.md).

## Props

| Prop        | Type                   | Default | Description                                                           |
| ----------- | ---------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `asChild`   | `boolean`              | `false` | Render the child element instead of a `<span>` (Radix `Slot`)         |
| `focusable` | `boolean`              | `false` | Show the content while it, or something inside it, has keyboard focus |
| `className` | `string`               |         | Merged with `sr-only`                                                 |
| `ref`       | `Ref<HTMLSpanElement>` |         |                                                                       |

Every other `<span>` prop (`id`, `lang`, …) is passed through. The element has `data-slot="visually-hidden"`.

## Accessibility

- Hidden text is part of the accessible name of whatever contains it: a button with only an icon and `VisuallyHidden` text is named by that text. Mark the icon `aria-hidden` (Onu's `Icon` does this when it has no `label`).
- Prefer `aria-label` when the whole name is hidden and the element supports it; use `VisuallyHidden` when you add to visible text ("Read more" + " about passport fees") or need real content such as a heading.
- Never hide focusable content without `focusable`: a keyboard user would land on something they cannot see (WCAG 2.4.7). With `focusable`, the content shows while it has focus.
- Hidden text is translated like any other text: pass the string from `t()` and add `lang` when it differs from the page.

---

<!-- docs/accessibility/live-region.md -->

# LiveRegion

An `aria-live` region: screen readers read its text whenever it changes, without moving focus. Use it for status that changes while the user stays where they are: "3 results", "Saved", "2 of 5 files uploaded". It is visually hidden by default; set `visible` to show the same text on screen.

```tsx
import { LiveRegion } from "@javaabu/onu"

// Hidden: only screen readers hear it
<LiveRegion>{copied ? t("input.copied") : null}</LiveRegion>

// A visible status line whose changes are announced
<LiveRegion role="status" visible as="p" className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">
  {done} of {total} files uploaded
</LiveRegion>

// Interrupts: only for errors that need attention now
<LiveRegion politeness="assertive">{error}</LiveRegion>
```

To announce a message from an event handler (and repeat the same message), use [`useAnnouncer`](./use-announcer.md), which renders a `LiveRegion` for you.

## Props

| Prop         | Type                                                   | Default                                        | Description                                                               |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `politeness` | `"polite" \| "assertive"`                              | `"polite"` (`"assertive"` with `role="alert"`) | `polite` waits until the screen reader is idle; `assertive` interrupts it |
| `atomic`     | `boolean`                                              | `true`                                         | Read the whole region on every change, not just the part that changed     |
| `role`       | `"status" \| "alert" \| "log" \| "timer" \| "marquee"` |                                                | Optional ARIA role (see below)                                            |
| `as`         | `"span" \| "div" \| "p"`                               | `"span"`                                       | Element to render; a `span` can sit inside a button or a paragraph        |
| `visible`    | `boolean`                                              | `false`                                        | Show the text on screen instead of hiding it with `sr-only`               |
| `children`   | `ReactNode`                                            |                                                | The current message; render `null` or `""` when there is nothing to say   |

Every other `<div>` prop (`id`, `className`, `lang`, …) is passed through. The element has `data-slot="live-region"`.

## Accessibility

- **Keep it mounted.** Screen readers watch regions that are already on the page. A region that mounts together with its text is often not read, so render the `LiveRegion` empty and change its children. Conditionally rendering the whole region (`{error && <LiveRegion>…`) defeats it.
- **Polite by default.** `assertive` cuts off whatever the user is hearing; keep it for errors that block them. `role="alert"` makes the region assertive unless you set `politeness`.
- **Roles.** A role is optional: `aria-live` alone is enough. `role="status"` lets assistive technology list the region as the page's status; leave it out when the page already has other `status` regions (a spinner, a toast), so tests and tools that look one up by role find the right one.
- **Short and specific.** Announce the result ("Row moved to position 3 of 8"), not the action ("Moving…"). Translate the text and keep it in the page's language.
- **Repeating a message.** Setting the same text again is not a change, so it is not read again. [`useAnnouncer`](./use-announcer.md) clears and re-sets it for you.

---

<!-- docs/accessibility/use-announcer.md -->

# useAnnouncer and announce

Announces messages to screen-reader users: "Row moved to position 3", "Settings saved", "4 results". `useAnnouncer` gives a component its own [`LiveRegion`](./live-region.md) and an `announce(message)` function; `announce()` does the same from anywhere through one page-wide region. Onu's sortable lists, reorderable tables, Kanban board, data table, editable grid, dual listbox, quick-create selects and map components use `useAnnouncer`.

```tsx
import { announce, useAnnouncer } from "@javaabu/onu"

function SortableRows({ rows }: { rows: Row[] }) {
  const { t } = useTranslation()
  const { announce, region } = useAnnouncer()
  const move = (from: number, to: number) => {
    onMove(from, to)
    announce(t("listing.movedToPosition", { name: rows[from].name, position: to + 1, total: rows.length }))
  }
  return <>…{region}</>
}

// Outside a component, or where there is nowhere to render a region:
await saveSettings()
announce("Settings saved")
announce("Connection lost", { politeness: "assertive" })
```

## Parameters

`useAnnouncer(options?)` takes the [`LiveRegion` props](./live-region.md#props) for its region (without `children`):

| Option       | Type                                                   | Default    | Description                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | ------------------------------- |
| `politeness` | `"polite" \| "assertive"`                              | `"polite"` |                                 |
| `role`       | `"status" \| "alert" \| "log" \| "timer" \| "marquee"` |            | e.g. `"status"`                 |
| `atomic`     | `boolean`                                              | `true`     |                                 |
| `visible`    | `boolean`                                              | `false`    | Show the last message on screen |
| `className`  | `string`                                               |            | Classes for the region          |

`announce(message, options?)` takes `{ politeness?: "polite" | "assertive" }` (default `polite`).

## Returns

`useAnnouncer` returns:

| Field      | Type                        | Description                                                         |
| ---------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `announce` | `(message: string) => void` | Puts `message` in the region. The same message twice is read twice. |
| `clear`    | `() => void`                | Empties the region                                                  |
| `message`  | `string`                    | The text in the region now, e.g. to pass to a region you render     |
| `region`   | `ReactElement`              | The `LiveRegion`. Render it once and keep it mounted.               |

`announce()` returns nothing.

## How repeats work

A screen reader reads a live region when its text changes. A new message is set straight away. The same message again is first cleared, then set 100 ms later, so "Row moved to position 2" twice in a row is read twice. A newer message cancels a pending repeat, and nothing is set after the component unmounts.

`announce()` keeps one hidden region per politeness level at the end of `<body>` (`data-onu-announcer="polite"` / `"assertive"`), created on first use. Its first message is set 100 ms after the region is created, since a region that appears with its text is often not read. The region is hidden with inline styles, so it does not depend on the `sr-only` utility being in your CSS.

## Accessibility

- Announce what happened, not what is happening, and keep it short: "Jane Doe moved to Approved", "3 files added". Translate it with `t()`.
- Use announcements for changes the user cannot see from where their focus is. When focus moves to the change (a dialog opens, an error field is focused), the screen reader already reads it; announcing too would read it twice.
- Prefer `useAnnouncer` inside components: the region is part of the component, so it inherits the component's `lang` and `dir` and is removed with it. Use `announce()` from non-React code, or from handlers that run as a component unmounts (after "Delete", for example).
- Use `politeness: "assertive"` only for messages that must interrupt, such as a lost connection.
- Visible status text (a "Saving…" label, an upload count) can be a [`LiveRegion`](./live-region.md) with `visible` instead of a separate announcement.

---

<!-- docs/form-scaffolding/form.md -->

# Form

A `<form>` that handles the boring parts: label layout for every field, disabling fields while saving, server validation errors (Laravel 422) under each field, an error summary at the top, and moving focus to the first invalid field. Works on its own, with Inertia, or with [react-hook-form](https://react-hook-form.com).

```tsx
import { Form, FormField, SubmitButton, TextInput } from "@javaabu/onu"

;<Form onSubmit={(values) => api.post("/users", values)} labelLayout="inline">
  <FormField label="Name" name="name" required>
    <TextInput />
  </FormField>
  <FormField label="Email" name="email" required>
    <TextInput type="email" />
  </FormField>
  <SubmitButton>Save</SubmitButton>
</Form>
```

## Submitting

`onSubmit(values, event)` gets the form's values: from react-hook-form when `form` is set, otherwise from `FormData` (repeated names such as `tags[]` become arrays). It may return a promise; until it settles:

- the form is `aria-busy`, every field is disabled (`disableWhileProcessing`), and
- `SubmitButton` shows a spinner and ignores clicks, so the form cannot be submitted twice.

Without `onSubmit` the form submits natively (`action` / `method`).

## Validation errors

When `onSubmit` throws or rejects with a Laravel validation error, the form:

1. shows each message under its field (fields are matched by `name`, so `items[0][name]` reads `items.0.name`);
2. moves focus to the first invalid field (opening a collapsed [`Fieldset`](./fieldset.md) if needed);
3. shows the [error summary](./validation-summary.md) at the top, with a link to every field.

These all count as a validation error:

```ts
throw { message: "…", errors: { email: ["The email has already been taken."] } } // the 422 body
throw axiosError // error.response.data is the 422 body
throw response // a fetch Response with status 422 (the JSON body is read)
throw new ValidationError({ email: "Taken" }) // no HTTP client needed
```

Any other error shows "The form could not be submitted." in the summary. Editing a field clears its server error. `onError(error, payload)` and `onSuccess(result)` are called after each attempt.

### Inertia

Pass Inertia's state straight through. New `errors` move focus to the first invalid field.

```tsx
const form = useForm({ name: "", email: "" })

<Form onSubmit={() => form.post("/users")} errors={form.errors} processing={form.processing}>
  …
</Form>
```

### react-hook-form

Pass the `useForm()` result as `form`. The form renders `FormProvider`, submits through `handleSubmit`, shows react-hook-form's errors in fields and in the summary, and maps server errors with `setError`.

```tsx
const form = useForm<Values>({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) })

<Form form={form} onSubmit={(values) => api.put(`/users/${id}`, values)}>
  <FormField label="Title" name="title">
    <TextInput {...form.register("title")} />
  </FormField>
  <SubmitButton />
</Form>
```

## Props

| Prop                     | Type                                 | Default   | Description                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `onSubmit`               | `(values, event) => unknown`         |           | Submit handler; may return a promise. Without it the form submits natively. |
| `form`                   | `UseFormReturn`                      |           | react-hook-form integration                                                 |
| `errors`                 | `Record<string, string \| string[]>` |           | Server errors (e.g. Inertia `form.errors`), merged with errors from submit  |
| `processing`             | `boolean`                            |           | Processing state from outside (e.g. Inertia `form.processing`)              |
| `labelLayout`            | `'stacked' \| 'inline'`              | provider  | Label layout for every field                                                |
| `disabled`               | `boolean`                            | `false`   | Disable every field                                                         |
| `disableWhileProcessing` | `boolean`                            | `true`    | Disable fields while processing                                             |
| `summary`                | `boolean`                            | `true`    | Show the error summary at the top                                           |
| `summaryTitle`           | `ReactNode`                          | generated | Summary heading                                                             |
| `focusOnError`           | `boolean`                            | `true`    | Focus the first invalid field when errors arrive                            |
| `onSuccess`              | `(result) => void`                   |           | After `onSubmit` resolves                                                   |
| `onError`                | `(error, payload \| null) => void`   |           | After `onSubmit` fails; `payload` is the validation body, if any            |
| `classNames`             | `{ summary }`                        |           | Classes for the summary                                                     |

All other `<form>` props are passed through, and `ref` points at the `<form>`. The form has `data-status="idle | submitting | success | error"`.

## Hooks and helpers

- `useOnuForm()`: `{ processing, status, errors, formError, setErrors(errors, message?), formRef }` of the nearest `Form`, or `null`.
- `getValidationErrors(value)` / `readValidationErrors(value)` (async, also reads a fetch `Response`): find a `{ message, errors }` payload in a thrown value.
